newsitem.title: UK: Britain declares victory over EU borders.
newsitem.headline: Britain declares victory over EU borders.

text.p: Britain declared a small victory on Tuesday after the chairman of the group negotiating a new European Union treaty conceded he did not expect London to lift passport controls along with its EU partners.

Dutch European Affairs Minister Michiel Patijn told a news conference earlier on Tuesday that it was a "political fact" that neither the current British government nor a future one would budge on the issue of border controls.
"We welcome the recognition by Patijn that the U.K. maintains the right to control its own borders," said David Davies, a minister for foreign affairs.

"This reflects the determined approach the government has taken on this issue throughout the intergovernmental conference negotiations and shows recognition by the other member states of the importance Britain attaches to keeping its own frontier controls."

The Netherlands, which currently holds the revolving EU presidency, proposed on Monday that the Schengen agreement lifting passport controls among members be brought into the EU treaty when a new one is agreed later this year.

It said that representatives from Britain and Ireland would be allowed to sit in on discussions but not to take part, while officials from Norway and Iceland, two non-EU members that have cooperation pacts with Schengen countries, could be given an active role.

Patijn, who emphasised he was speaking personally, said he saw no reason if Schengen was part of the EU why Britain and Ireland could not participate in the sharing of police data without lifting their border controls.
Britain believes that it needs to maintain its own border controls to keep out illegal immigrants, drugs and other threats.

The government has consistently taken a tough line on aspects of EU policy it does not agree with. Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher won Britain the right to opt out of the Social Chapter which lays down employment conditions and the present government has refused to commit itself to joining a planned single currency.
